commentary_title: Weakness in utilisation persists
commentary_summary: The utilisation of Capesize vessels stayed on a downward trajectory despite a strong start to the year. | The global tonne-mile index complemented the weakness in the market, registering a WoW decline. However, the index remained much higher than the levels achieved last year in the same period. | As China's Lunar New Year Holidays begin, activity in the market has slowed down, particularly affecting Capesize demand. | The congestion in China's load ports has eased while the congestion at the country's discharge ports remains modest as compared to last two years.

commentary_title: Surge in vessel utilisation
commentary_summary: The utilisation of Capesize vessels surged, registering a rise of one percentage point in a week. The resulting level of utilisation was much higher compared to last year. | Despite the high supply of ballast vessels in the Atlantic, high demand due to strong export volumes on long-haul routes such as Brazil-China and West Africa-China, raised employment of vessels. | The tonnage underway in the West surged to historically high levels, with approximately 70 mdwt moving in the region. | Meanwhile, the global tonne-mile index moderated WoW but continues to be high YoY. China’s iron ore inventories remain low YoY, with import for restocking aiding demand.

commentary_title: Ample supply weighing down rates
commentary_summary: The utilisation of Capesize vessels decreased after reaching substantially high levels last month. The tonnage underway in the West has been historically as well as unseasonally high in April. | The expansion in the supply stretch avaialble in the market rose primarily due to the rise in ballast vessels that are drifitng in the sea. | The ballast speed in the West remained low amid ample supply in the Atlantic. As a result, the spot rates have started to normalise. | Meanwhile, the tonnemile index remains significantly high YoY despite slight moderation last week. Buoyant demand in China has pushed the employability of vessels, as a result of which, 13.4 mdwt tonnage is waiting to unload at the country's discharge ports.

commentary_title: Surge in Drewry's tonnemile index
commentary_summary: Drewry's tonnemile index for Capesize vessels surged last week, rising 8% WoW and 31% YoY. | The share of laden vessels continues to be on an uptrend in the East, with a 9.3 percentage point increase MoM. | China's buoyant appetite for iron ore and coal is aiding the demand for Capesize vessels. Despite sluggish steel production, the country has been accumulating iron ore due to rake in the benefit of subdued prices, supporting demand on the Brazil-China and Australia-China routes. | Amid the already high demand for coal in the country, the share of Australia has edged up MoM. Since the majority of Australia's coal exports to China are shipped on Capesize vessels, their employment has risen.

commentary_title: Capesize utilisation inches up
commentary_summary: The utilisation of Capesize vessels rose to 93.3% from 92.7% the previous week due to heightened industrial activity in India and China, driving steady demand for iron ore and coking coal. | Additionally, the Capesize tonne mile index has surged to 108.1, an increase of 7.5 basis points W-o-W, as the demand for Capesize vessels on the Guinea-China bauxite route rose, driven by a substantial expansion in Chinese domestic aluminium consumption. Overall, the industrial surge in key regions has significantly boosted the demand and utilisation of Capesize vessels, reflecting a robust market for bulk commodities.

commentary_title: Higher YoY demand for Capesize vessels
commentary_summary: The utilisation of Capesize vessels continued on the downward trend for the second consecutive week, reaching close to the lowest levels seen in last two months. | The dampening of utilisation levels can be attributed to the upswing in the global ballast speed, which reached its highest level seen in the last two months. | The share of laden vessels continued to be buoyant in the East as well as the West regions, signalling higher employment of vessels due to expansion in iron ore and bauxite demand. | Guinea's rising bauxite exports are a critical driver for the upsurge in Capesize employment. The exports surged by 22% YoY in June, a notable increase despite the typical summer decline caused by the rainy season. This has also contributed to the buoyant tonnemile index in 2024 compared to 2023.

commentary_title: Moderation in utilisation of Capesize vessels
commentary_summary: The utilisation of Capesize vessels declined marginally last week to reach 91.7% from 91.9% the week before. | Meanwhile, the tonnemile index continued to be on a downward trend, declining for the third consecutive week. However, the market continues to perform well YoY. | The ballast tonnage at anchor in the Atlantic has been modest as the onset of monsoon disrupts loading activity in Guinea, dampening bauxite trade in this season. | China's iron ore inventory for 2024 peaked in end-June, which has moderated additional imports in July, reducing the ballast tonnage wiating to load in Australia and Brazil.

commentary_title: Decline in utilisation
commentary_summary: The Capesize vessel utilization declined last week, reversing the upward trend of the previous three weeks. The drop in global ballast speed squeezed the supply in the market, dampening utilisation. | The tonne-mile index rose marginally but continues to be much higher than last year's level. Iron ore sockpiling activity by China has been aiding Capesize demand as iron ore prices continue to be subdued. The expansion in the share of laden vessels in the East compared to last year corroborates the high demand. | Meanwhile, the proportion of laden vessels is subdued in the West as more vessels load at Brazil and Guinea and head towards the East. The global moving average of the tonnage waiting at the anchor has been subdued lately and is likely to ease freight rates in the short-term with the ease in congestion.

commentary_title: Capesize Utilisation Drops Amid Slowdown in Laden Speed
commentary_summary: The laden speed declined in the Western and Eastern hemispheres for the second consecutive week | The ballast tonnage at anchor in the Indian Ocean fell significantly within a week, from 2.0 mdwt to 1.5 mdwt | This is attributed to reduced iron ore trade on the India-China route due to low demand in China, which resulted in fewer loading activities in India | On the contrary, the global tonne-mile index for Capesizes improved last week and remained significantly high YoY. Buoyant bauxite demand in China has pushed the employability of vessels, resulting in about 12.5 mdwt of cargo waiting to unload at the country's discharge ports

commentary_title: Rise in utilisation as speed increases
commentary_summary: Capesize vessel utilisation rose marginally last week from 91% to 91.2%, though it remains much lower YoY. The increase in global ballast speed contributed to WoW improvement in utilisation. | Additionally, the tonne-mile index expanded, driven by robust iron ore shipments from Brazil and Australia. | Amid the growing demand for coal, Australian exports to China have edged up, further supporting the steady employment of Capesize vessels on this route. This resulted in higher tonnage waiting at the anchor in Oceania's load ports compared to last week.

commentary_title: Decline in Capesize utilisation
commentary_summary: The utilisation of Capesize vessels shrank 0.2 percentage point from the previous week, but still remained substantially lower than the level in 2023. | The ballast speed in the West as well as in the East reduced significantly due to lower iron ore loadings from Brazil and Australia and fewer coal cargoes into Europe. | Meanwhile, laden tonnage at anchor in China plunged this week, from 12.6 mdwt to 11.4 mdwt, due to reduced iron ore and coal imports amid sufficient stockpiles.

commentary_title: Holiday season impacts Capesize earnings. Tightening tonnage provided some boost.
commentary_summary: The global Capesize utilisation increased to 95.2% compared to 2024. | The Capsize tonne-miles index experienced a 1.6% WoW decline, reaching 109 points. This decline can be attributed to the seasonally low market activity as the Pacific region enters the Lunar New Year holidays. This seasonal slowdown is further evidenced by reduced laden tonnage at anchor in China. | The share of laden vessels in both East and West regions declined WoW. In tandem, reduced enquiries for iron ore shipments from Brazil to China translated into spot rates declining by 3% WoW, reaching $17.4 per tonne on the benchmark Brazil-China route.

commentary_title: Capesize utilisation and Baltic rates decline
commentary_summary: The global Capesize utilisation declined to 92.2% WoW. Meanwhile, the Capesize tonne-miles index also experienced a 3.4% WoW decline, primarily due to the seasonally low market. Baltic rates are also in tandem with declining utilisation. | Additionally, the laden tonnage at anchorage in Oceania also declined dropping to a mere 0.2 mdwt after reaching a historical high of 1.2 mdwt in January. | The share of laden vessels in East and West regions declined WoW, reaching historically low levels.

commentary_title: Utilisation remained stable, Capesize ballast speed plunged
commentary_summary: Global Capesize utilisation increased a marginal 0.2 percentage points WoW to 92.1%, but it was down 1.5% YoY for week 9. In contrast, the tonne-miles index remained stable at 100.4, marking a 13% YoY increase. | Laden tonnage at anchorage in China declined nearly 30%, possibly due to the country's plans to cut steel production which will weigh on iron ore demand. Market estimates indicate that iron ore imports fell to a record low in February, the lowest since 2019, which has potentially led to reduced loadings on Capesize vessels. | Ballast speed crashed 15% compared to two weeks prior when it was at a record high. Laden speed also declined in tandem, with 4.3% WoW.

commentary_title: Global Capesize recovery continues
commentary_summary: Capesize utilisation continues to recover, marking its fourth consecutive week of improvement. It increased by 0.3 percentage points, reaching 92.5%. The Tonne-miles index also showed this positive movement in tandem. | In March, ballast vessel days at anchor fell by almost 9%, while global ballast speed increased in the Western regions, suggesting that more vessels are actively seeking employment, with tonnage underway rising WoW in the west. | Laden Tonnage at anchor in China and India has been trending downward due to a decrease in their seaborne imports of coking coal over the past month. This decline is further supported by a recent reduction in India's thermal coal imports.

commentary_title: Capesize tonne mile index drops amid declining vessel speed
commentary_summary: The Capesize tonne-miles index declined by 4.3% in week 19 in tandem with reduced ballast and laden speeds; a decrease in Baltic rates followed. | The percentage of laden vessels in the West decreased in accordance with declining spot rates on the Brazil-China route. | Vessels at Anchor in the East decreased by 20% MoM, accompanied by reduced laden congestion in the region. | China's laden tonnage has decreased due to a reduction in coal imports. This decline is attributed to slower growth in power consumption and increased coal inventories within the country.

commentary_title: Capesize markets soars amid robust iron ore trade
commentary_summary: The Capesize tonne-miles index experienced a strong upward trend, rising by 26% over the past two weeks. Increased iron ore trade volumes from Brazil and Australia drove this growth. This led to an increase in Baltic 5TC rates. | The Laden Tonnage at Anchor for China showed an uptick in Week 23, signalling increased demand from the Far East, particularly China. Higher Capesize loadings from Australia primarily fueled this surge, as iron ore exports to China remain robust. | This trend is further supported by increased ballast speeds in the east. Meanwhile, the rise in Australian iron ore shipments to India has led to growing congestion at Indian ports during Week 23, reflecting logistical challenges amid the higher cargo volumes.

commentary_title: Capesize Tonne-Mile weakness reflects dwindling Chinese demand
commentary_summary: Tonne-mile demand for Capesize vessels dipped 1.3% in Week 27, largely due to a fall in Chinese iron ore imports driven by weakening steel demand. | Ballast tonnage in the Atlantic continued its downtrend, nearing historically low levels since 2023. This reflects softer loadings from Brazil to China due to reduced manufacturing activity in China. | Spot rates on the Brazil-China route dropped 13.7% WoW, further pressured by Australia's forecast of declining iron ore export revenues amid China's weak steel demand and lower production levels.

commentary_title: Capesize market shows signs of strength in 2H25
commentary_summary: Capesize utilisation has begun to recover in 2H25, rising by 2 percentage points since mid-July after a subdued 1H25. This rebound aligns with a softening in Baltic rates earlier in the year, which are now improving alongside utilisation. The gains have been driven by increased activity on the Brazil-China and Transpacific routes. | Despite temporary disruptions from cyclones and flooding in early 2025, Australia’s miners maintained robust iron ore exports, with nearly 85% of shipments heading to China which supported Spot rates on the Brazil- China route to surge 27% MoM in 2H25.

commentary_title: Capesize market strengthens supported by rising Congestion
commentary_summary: The Capesize tonne-miles index rose 2% WoW in week 37, with utilisation, laden speed, and Baltic benchmark rates all moving higher in tandem. | The vessel capacity at anchor in the West rose 12.8% MoM in September, as fewer ships moved underway. The higher share of laden vessels in the West further supported spot rates, which continued their steady upward trend. | While ballast congestion in the Pacific remained flat, the Atlantic saw a consistent uptrend. Laden congestion stayed elevated across both the Pacific and Oceania, with nearing historically high levels in Oceania.

commentary_title: Capesize segment gains momentum
commentary_summary: Capesize utilisation saw a modest uptick in Week 40, supported by higher tonne- miles and an increase in vessels waiting at anchor across both East and West regions. Global ballast and laden speeds also trended higher, reflecting stronger market activity. | Weather disruptions from recent typhoons tightened short-term supply, as vessel schedules were delayed, leading to increased laden congestion at Chinese and other East Asian ports. | Seasonal strength in Q3 iron ore exports from Brazil further supported the market, with spot rates on the Brazil–China route rising and congestion levels increasing, signalling improving sentiment in the Capesize segment.

commentary_title: Steady production of iron ore keeps the utilisation up
commentary_summary: The Capesize utilisation edged up slightly to 92.5% in week 44, with a 27.2% fall in vessel capacity at port MoM in the West. Alongside this, vessel capacity at anchor is falling, leading to reduced congestion. | Vale reported its strongest quarterly output in 3Q25, driven by record production from the S11D project and continued ramp-ups across other operations. YTD performance keeps the company on track to meet the upper end, supported by higher sales volumes. | Strong Brazilian exports to long-haul Asian markets are expected to sustain tonne-mile demand and increase Capesize activity through remianing year. | In the Pacific, steady demand from miners supported gradual gains in the latter half of the week, while in the Atlantic, a tightening tonnage list provided support to fronthaul trades. The announcement of a one-year US- China trade truce further lifted market sentiment.

commentary_title: Capesize market tightens as Utilisation and rates strengthen
commentary_summary: Capesize utilisation strengthened notably, rising to 92.5% from 92.2% WoW, reflecting firmer trade activity. This uplift was accompanied by a sharp rally in freight rates on the benchmark C5TC index, marking the strongest increase since December 2023. | The surge was primarily driven by robust front-haul demand, including higher iron ore shipments from Brazil and increased bauxite exports from Guinea, which collectively absorbed more tonnage and supported higher utilisation and spot rates. | Vessel operating patterns also signalled tightening supply, with laden speeds remaining steady, ballast speeds edged higher, reaching their highest level this year, indicating owners repositioning to capture stronger market opportunities.

commentary_title: Atlantic weakness offsets Pacific demand in Capesize market
commentary_summary: The Capesize segment weakened during the week, with tonne-miles index falling slightly WoW to 95.6, while Baltic C5TC rates fell in tandem. Ballast speed also declined alongside falling laden speed. Spot rates also fell on major Capesize routes, including the Brazil-China route. | Capesize activity improved in the Pacific with Ballast congestion increasing as major miners remained active in the market, helping to support cargo volumes. However, despite firm cargo demand in the Pacific, the Atlantic market softened with laden congestion falling to YTD lowest levels as vessel availability increased. A growing tonnage list weighed on freight rates, limiting upside momentum and creating a divergence between the two basins. | The combined impact of Middle East-related vessel delays and congestion at West African ports has removed part of the fleet from active trading. Although a very small capacity is directly affected, these inefficiencies continue to tighten effective vessel supply.

commentary_title: Softer Capesize freight market despite resilient Iron ore trade
commentary_summary: The Capesize market softened in Week 29, with utilisation declining to around 92%, along with the C5TC declining to $33,653. While the vessel fixing activity remained healthy, particularly in the Pacific, the available fleet increased across both basins, preventing cargo demand from sustaining the stronger momentum seen in previous weeks. | The Pacific remained active, with all major miners in the market, but rates declined as cargo volumes were insufficient to absorb the growing availability of vessels. In the Atlantic, the North Atlantic fleet list continued to increase, limiting activity and weighing on freight levels despite stable cargo demand. In contrast, the South Atlantic remained relatively resilient, with the C3 Brazil-China route rising above $33/tonne. | Rio Tinto's 2Q26 Pilbara iron ore sales exceeded market expectations, with first- half shipments rising YoY, pointing towards expectations of stronger Australian export volumes in the 2H26. Although higher diesel prices linked to Middle East tensions have increased mining costs, continued iron ore exports from Australia are expected to provide support for Capesize tonne-mile demand in the coming months.

commentary_title: Pacific correction offsets the resilient Atlantic region in Capesize market
commentary_summary: The Capesize utilisation fell to 92.1% following a 12% decline in Baltic benchmark C5TC rates over the last two weeks. The Pacific region was the main source of weakness as Chinese ports reopened following Typhoon Dolphin, allowing previously stuck vessels to return to the market. With vessel availability increasing faster than cargo demand, spot rates on Australia-China C5 fell sharply from above $16/tonne to around $14/tonne by the end of the week. | The reopening of Chinese ports released vessels delayed by Typhoon Dolphin, easing Pacific congestion and increasing available tonnage. Greater vessel availability intensified competition for cargoes, with some owners increasingly ballasting toward the Atlantic, where C3 remained more stable. This is likely to keep Pacific rates under pressure in the near term, while slower speeds and repositioning flows may support Atlantic availability. | South Brazil and West Africa–China routes continued to provide support, with C3 holding around $36/tonne having fewer ballasting vessels, and healthy first-half September demand helped offset softer sentiment elsewhere.

commentary_title: Strong demand meets tighter effective supply in the Capesize market
commentary_summary: The Drewry's Tonne-miles index for Capesize is on an uptrend, rising 2.8% WoW, reaching 98 in week 37. C5TC faced some correction WoW as the early-week Pacific rally lost momentum. C5 (Australia-China), however, remained firm, supported by strong miner participation and healthy demand for vessels. The willingness of miners to cover multiple vessels has kept the market well supported. | North China port closures due to strong winds and ongoing operational disruptions have delayed vessel schedules and reduced fleet efficiency. At the same time, higher bunker prices are encouraging owners to factor in higher fuel costs in voyage economics. | C3 levels (Brazil-China route) held around $41–42 per tonne, supported by limited available vessels and fresh October demand, with owners maintaining firm offers. However, elevated freight rates are increasingly challenging the economics of commodities. This could limit further upside if Atlantic demand softens, although the relatively short vessel list continues to put a cap.
